summary: On 18 December 2023 the European Commission opened the first formal Digital Services Act (DSA) investigation, targeting Elon Musk's X. The probe covers illegal content risk management, content moderation, the Community Notes system, transparency and researcher data access, and deceptive design around Blue checks. X says it is cooperating, while the article frames the case as a test of EU enforcement resolve and Musk's willingness to clash with regulators.
one_line: The European Commission opened the first formal DSA investigation, into Elon Musk's X, over illegal content, moderation, transparency and deceptive Blue check design.
key_facts: The European Commission announced a formal proceeding against X on 18 December 2023, the first confirmed investigation under the Digital Services Act (DSA).
The probe examines possible breaches on risk management, content moderation, dark patterns, advertising transparency and data access for researchers.
In October the Commission sent X an "urgent" formal request for information about its response to information risks from the Israel-Hamas war, with a deadline of the end of October.
The Commission's preliminary investigation drew on X's risk assessment report submitted in September, its Transparency report published on 3 November, and replies to a formal request for information.
One focus is the effectiveness of X's "Community Notes" crowdsourced fact-checking system and related policies mitigating risks to civic discourse and electoral processes.
The Commission suspects shortcomings in X giving researchers access to publicly accessible data as mandated by Article 40 of the DSA, and in its ads repository.
The Commission also suspects deceptive design in X's user interface, notably the checkmarks linked to subscription products, the so-called Blue checks.
If proven, the failures would breach Articles 34(1), 34(2), 35(1), 16(5), 16(6), 25(1), 39 and 40(12) of the DSA, and the EU will investigate "as a matter of priority".
X was designated a very large online platform (VLOP) under the DSA in April; confirmed breaches can bring fines of up to 6% of global annual turnover.
The EU can apply interim measures where there is a risk of serious harm and may even seek to have access to infringing services temporarily blocked; there is no confirmed timeline for the probe.

X's Joe Benarroch, brought in by CEO Linda Yaccarino to work on business operations, said X remains committed to complying with the DSA and is cooperating, and that the process should remain free of political influence.
The probe comes shortly after a complaint against X's adtech by privacy rights group noyb, though the two are unlikely to be directly linked.
X recently started a research program giving outsiders data on systemic risks on the platform in the EU, but the Commission doubts it meets the DSA's transparency bar.
